problem:
Brightfield Energy has collected the same monthly bill twice from 300 customers after a billing re-run duplicated a batch. The money has already settled, so the collections cannot be cancelled or revoked. Customers are calling, the support team is offering to delete the duplicate collections from the system, and finance is worried that deleting settled entries will break reconciliation. Everyone agrees the customers must be paid back, but nobody agrees on the mechanism that does it correctly.

A reversal is not a deletion and it is not a refund claim by the debtor. It is a separate, linked transaction initiated by the creditor after settlement, within a defined scheme window, for a defined reason, for the same or a corrected amount. It leaves the original settlement record intact and creates its own audit trail, so the duplicate can be traced from the billing error through the reversal to the customer account.

Brightfield Energy needs a reversal process that checks eligibility first, creates exactly one reversal per original, posts it correctly, and tells the customer precisely what was reversed and when the money will be back.
solution:
Treat reversal as a controlled financial event with four checks before it is created. Check one, eligibility: the collection has settled, the reversal is initiated by the creditor, and the reason is one the scheme permits, such as a duplicate collection or an incorrect amount. Check two, timing: a reversal is only available from the settlement date and within 5 Inter-PSP Business Days following the due date, so the team must confirm the window is still open before promising the customer a reversal. Check three, linkage: the reversal references the original instruction ID, mandate reference and amount, and carries a reason code that explains the error. Check four, uniqueness: the system blocks a second reversal for the same original unless a partial reversal is explicitly permitted and recorded.

The reversal is posted as a separate transaction, normally carried by pacs.004, and the original settlement entry is never edited or deleted. The debtor is notified with the original amount, the reversed amount, the reason and the expected value date. Where the window has already closed, the team does not force a reversal through; it uses the available alternative, such as a separate creditor-to-debtor credit transfer or a commercial refund, and records why the scheme reversal was not available.

The process also distinguishes a reversal from a debtor refund. A refund is claimed by the debtor through the debtor PSP under the Core or B2B refund rights, with the Core authorised refund available within 8 weeks of the debit date and an unauthorised claim within 13 months, while B2B has no authorised refund right. A reversal is initiated by the creditor. Mixing the two up sends the customer to the wrong channel and delays the correction.

decision.question: Brightfield Energy duplicated 300 collections and they have settled. The duplicate amounts are identical to the originals and the due date was four Inter-PSP Business Days ago. The learner must decide the correct remedy.

options.label: A
options.detail: Initiate a linked reversal for each duplicate collection within the scheme window, using pacs.004, and notify each debtor.

options.label: B
options.detail: Delete the duplicate collection records from the billing system so they disappear.

options.label: C
options.detail: Send a camt.056 cancellation request for each duplicate collection.

options.label: D
options.detail: Ask each of the 300 debtors to claim an authorised refund from their own bank.

decisionRationale: Option A is correct because a settled duplicate is corrected by a creditor-initiated reversal, linked to the original, within the scheme window. Option B is wrong because deleting a settled record destroys the audit trail and breaks reconciliation. Option D is wrong because it pushes a creditor error onto debtors and uses the wrong mechanism. Option C is wrong because cancellation applies before settlement, not after it.

steps.title: Discovers the duplicate billing run and identifies the 300 duplicate collections with their original references.
Confirms each duplicate has settled and checks the reversal window: from settlement date and within 5 Inter-PSP Business Days following the due date.
Creates one linked reversal per duplicate, with the original instruction reference, amount and reason code.
Submits the reversals as pacs.004 instructions into clearing.
Receives each reversal, validates the linkage, and credits the debtor account.
Matches each reversal to its original and updates both records as a linked pair.
Notifies each debtor of the duplicate, the reversed amount and the expected value date.
Reconciles originals against reversals and closes the incident with a full audit trail.

happy: The duplicate is found inside the reversal window. The team creates exactly one linked pacs.004 reversal per duplicate, each referencing its original instruction and carrying the duplicate reason code. The debtor PSPs credit the 300 debtors, the reversals match their originals one to one, and the customers receive a clear notice stating the duplicate amount and the value date. The original settlement records remain intact, the incident closes with no second reversal and no debtor refund claim, and the billing re-run control is fixed so the duplicate cannot recur.

negative.title: Reversal deadline missed
negative.detail: The error is found after 5 Inter-PSP Business Days following the due date. Do not force a scheme reversal. Use the available alternative, such as a separate creditor credit transfer, record why the reversal window had closed, and notify the debtor of the corrected route and date.

negative.title: Duplicate reversal
negative.detail: A re-run of the reversal job creates a second reversal for the same original. Block the second reversal on the original instruction ID, quarantine the duplicate request, and reconcile the reversal count against the original count before any further submission.

negative.title: Original already refunded
negative.detail: A debtor has already claimed a refund for the same collection before the reversal is sent. Detect the existing refund by the original reference, stop the reversal to avoid double repayment, and reconcile the refund as the correcting event with a linked record.

negative.title: Partial reversal amount dispute
negative.detail: Only part of the collected amount was wrong, and the reversal amount does not match the error. Reverse only the incorrect portion where the scheme permits a partial reversal, state the partial amount and reason clearly, and keep the correct portion settled with its own linked record.

technical: Model the reversal as a separate transaction with its own instruction ID, linked to the original by the original instruction ID and end-to-end ID, and enforce a uniqueness constraint so one original can have only the permitted number of reversals. Validate the reversal window in Inter-PSP Business Days from the settlement date and the due date before the reversal is created, and record the window check as an audit event. Carry the mandate reference, amount, currency, value date and reason code in the pacs.004, and never edit the original settlement record. Make the reversal posting idempotent on its own instruction ID so a retried submission cannot double-credit the debtor. Keep the reversal distinct from a debtor refund in the data model, with separate reason codes, initiators and status flows, so reporting never conflates the two.

accounting: The original collection stays posted as a settled credit to the creditor and a debit to the debtor. The reversal posts as a separate linked entry that debits the creditor operating account and credits the debtor, so the ledger shows both the error and the correction. The in-transit and settlement control accounts reconcile the reversal total against the duplicate total, and any unmatched reversal goes to an exception worklist with an owner and an SLA. Where a reversal is not possible because the window has closed, the alternative credit transfer is posted from a separate corrections account with its own reference, so it is never mixed into the scheme reversal totals. Operations reports reversal volumes, reasons and window breaches weekly, because a rising reversal rate is a billing control failure, not a normal cost of business.

scenarios.given: a settled collection eligible for reversal
scenarios.when: a valid reversal is submitted within the scheme window
scenarios.then: the reversal is linked to the original and posted once. the original settlement record remains unchanged

scenarios.given: a reversal request for an original that has already been refunded
scenarios.then: the second correction is blocked. the existing refund is recorded as the correcting event

questions.question: Within what window is an SDD reversal available?
options: Within 8 weeks of the debit date
Any time after the due date
Only from the settlement date and within 5 Inter-PSP Business Days following the due date
Within 13 months of the debit date
questions.explanation: A reversal is only available from the settlement date and within 5 Inter-PSP Business Days following the due date.

questions.question: How should a reversal be recorded?
options: By deleting the original settlement entry
As a separate linked transaction that leaves the original intact
questions.explanation: A reversal is a separate linked transaction. The original settlement record remains intact.

questions.question: Who initiates an SDD reversal?
questions.explanation: A reversal is initiated by the creditor, unlike a refund claim which is initiated by the debtor.

questions.question: What is the Core authorised refund period for a debtor?
questions.explanation: An authorised SDD Core refund is available within 8 weeks of the debit date, with no questions asked. An unauthorised claim runs to 13 months.
